description: We are a group of passionate technology enthusiasts interested in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Science, and software development. We enjoy exploring innovative ideas, solving real-world problems, and collaborating to turn challenges into practical solutions. Through NASA Space Apps, we aim to learn, share knowledge, gain hands-on experience, and create meaningful impact through technology. 🚀
summary:
We developed Field Shift, a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta.
The prototype combines NASA rainfall, temperature, soil-moisture, terrain and Landsat observations with Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA crop-suitability data. For a selected agricultural study cell, users can compare 13 crop-rotation options and adjust the importance of land suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local agricultural practice. The dashboard presents ranked alternatives, component scores and historical environmental context, making the comparison transparent rather than providing an unexplained recommendation.
Field Shift addresses the challenge by turning Earth observation data into an accessible tool for water-aware agricultural planning. It helps users explore how different priorities affect their choices and discuss alternatives with local experts. The current pilot covers Sidi Salem and Qallin using historical, processed data. It supports informed decisions without claiming live measurements, guaranteed yields or proven water savings.
details:
What we developed and how it works

Field Shift is a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta. Our prototype covers Sidi Salem and Qallin in Kafr El-Sheikh, using a grid of 560 approximately one-kilometre study cells, including 556 eligible agricultural cells.

Users select a study cell on the interactive map or enter a farm’s coordinates to match it to an eligible cell. The dashboard displays historical environmental indicators and compares 13 crop-rotation options involving wheat, sugar beet, potato, maize, rice, cotton, soybean and year-round alfalfa.

Each option receives three component scores: land suitability, modeled irrigation requirement and local agricultural practice. Users can adjust the importance of these criteria, and the system recalculates the ranking using a transparent weighted average. This lets users explore alternatives instead of accepting one unexplained recommendation.

Data and tools

We combined NASA POWER temperature data, GPM rainfall estimates, SMAP soil-moisture information, SRTM terrain data and NASA/USGS Landsat observations with ESA Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA GAEZ agricultural data. NASA resources provide environmental context, while GAEZ supplies crop-specific suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local-practice inputs.

The frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for interactive mapping. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, pandas and Pydantic for data handling, validation and scoring. We used pytest and HTTPX for automated testing, GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting. The prototype is software-based and requires no specialised hardware or field sensors.

AI tools supported planning, coding and debugging after our team independently developed the original project idea.

Benefits, creativity and intended impact

Field Shift makes complex environmental and agricultural information easier to explore through maps, historical indicators and explainable comparisons. Its creative approach connects Earth observation data with an interactive, farmer-facing workflow where users control their decision priorities.

Arabic support makes the interface more accessible to local users. Farm checklists and JSON report export help users organise their planning and share comparisons with agricultural advisors.

Our intended impact is to support better-informed, water-aware agricultural decisions—not replace farmers’ experience or local agricultural expertise.

Factors considered and current limitations

We considered water requirements, land suitability, established agricultural practice, usability, language accessibility and data quality. We also accounted for differences in dataset resolution and the uncertainty of historical and modeled information.

The current version is limited to the pilot area. Study cells are not surveyed farm parcels, irrigation estimates are not measured consumption, and saved farms and tasks remain in the user’s browser. We do not claim guaranteed yields, higher profits or proven water savings. Future development would focus on broader coverage, updated data, additional agronomic and economic factors, and field validation with farmers and specialists.
